# Introduction

Basketball players have traditionally been described by five positions, yet game-related statistics only partly separate these positions [@sampaio2006discriminant], and a growing literature replaces them with data-driven functional roles [@kalman2020lineup; @ibanez2025redefining; @chen2023modeling; @wei2025enhancing; @pendolareinecke2025exploring; @south2024basketball]. The number of roles reported varies widely between studies, and a recent systematic review attributed these differences largely to methodological heterogeneity and called for a unified, high-quality approach [@ribes2026identifying]. In the EuroLeague, data-driven work has documented the convergence of power forwards and centres [@konca2026from] and has modelled lineups with regularised plus-minus [@grassetti2020extended], but the full set of player roles has not been derived.

Two methodological gaps limit what role studies can claim. First, the number of roles is usually chosen with internal validity indices [@duman2021cluster], whereas the reproducibility of the partition under resampling [@hennig2007cluster] is seldom reported, and resampling rarely respects the fact that the same players appear in several seasons. Second, roles are frequently linked to team or lineup success [@kalman2020lineup; @chen2023modeling; @penner2025player], but lineup outcomes are noisy, lineups are short-lived, and the players who make up a successful role combination are often simply better players. Because lineup performance can be predicted from the quality of the individual players [@martonosi2023predicting], role effects need to be evaluated after player quality has been accounted for.

The aims of this study were therefore (1) to derive functional player roles for the EuroLeague from open data, choosing the number of roles by player-level bootstrap stability; (2) to quantify how far these roles cut across registered positions; and (3) to test whether the role composition of a lineup explains its performance beyond the individual quality of its players. Here we show that four or five roles can be recovered reproducibly, whereas finer partitions cannot; that ball handlers and rim protectors remain largely tied to registered positions whereas the other roles combine positions; and that an apparent effect of role composition on lineup performance beyond player quality is not robust once role information from the test period is excluded.
